property_summary: If this test contract locks a guess for an address, then calling lockInGuess again with 1 ether must revert (i.e., re-locking is disallowed).
Calling lockInGuess with 1 ether reverts iff the caller already has a guess recorded (i.e., re-locking is disallowed in the original).

On the original contract, calling lockInGuess with any parameters never reverts when the caller has no prior guess; the test asserts that if lockInGuess reverts then the caller must have had a prior guess (i.e., reverts imply a prior guess exists).

Calling lockInGuess with 1 ether never reverts for an address that currently has no guess recorded; i.e., if the call reverts then the caller must have already had a guess recorded (so for an address with no prior guess the call must succeed).

In the original contract, calling lockInGuess(...) with exactly 1 ether never reverts for a caller whose prior guess slot is zero, so: if the call reverts then the caller must already have had a nonzero stored block (i.e., had a prior guess); the mutated contract inverts this and will revert when the caller had no prior guess.

After calling lockInGuess with any payable value, the contract's balance decreases by exactly that value only if the call required exactly 1 ether (so for the original contract lockInGuess always reverts unless 1 ether is sent, preserving balances), hence for any sent value the caller's balance change equals zero unless value == 1 ether.
Calls to lockInGuess revert iff the call does not send exactly 1 ether.
For any caller and any value sent, if lockInGuess call does not revert then exactly 1 ether was sent (original requires msg.value==1 ether), so reverted == false implies amount == 1 ether.
If lockInGuess does not revert then the sent value must be exactly 1 ether (i.e., non-reverting calls only occur when amount == 1 ether).
For any caller and any sent amount, if lockInGuess does not revert then the contract's balance increases by exactly 1 ether (i.e., successful calls always transfer exactly 1 ether into C).

property_summary: After a successful lockInGuess call funded with 1 ether, the stored Guess.block for the caller must be strictly greater than the current block.number at the time of the call (i.e. reference stores block.number+1), but the mutant that stores block.number breaks this by storing a value not greater than the current block number for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully funds lockInGuess with 1 ether, the reference stores a guessed.block strictly greater than the block number at the time of staking (block.number+1), whereas the mutant that stores block.number can produce a stored guess.block that is not greater than the current block for some inputs (e.g., when settle is called in the next block this distinction causes different settle behavior).

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract stores guesses(caller).block equal to block.number+1 (strictly greater than the current block), while the mutant that stores block.number will produce a stored guesses(caller).block that is not > block.number for some fuzzed inputs (allowing the fuzzer to find such a case).

For any caller who funds lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always stores guesses(caller).block == block.number + 1 immediately after the call; the mutant that writes block.number can make guesses(caller).block != block.number + 1 for some fuzzed caller/block context.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always stores guesses(caller).block strictly greater than the block.number at which the call was made (block.number+1), whereas the mutant that writes block.number can store a guesses(caller).block that is NOT strictly greater than that block number for some inputs.

After calling lockInGuess(hash) with 1 ether from any caller, the stored guesses[caller].block in the correct contract is equal to block.number + 1 (i.e., a small positive uint representing a block number), while the mutant overwrites that field with the provided hash cast to uint256 so for some hash values the stored block will not equal block.number + 1; the test fuzzes the hash and caller to find such a discrepancy.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, after lockInGuess(hash) completes on the correct contract the stored guesses[caller].block is a small positive block number (specifically block.number + 1) and thus when read back via calling settle's precondition behavior (a subsequent call to settle must see guesses[caller].block != 0 and normally block.number <= guesses[caller].block may be false); the mutant can overwrite the block field with the provided hash cast to uint256 so for some fuzzed hash values the stored block will not equal a valid block number (e.g., it will be 0 or some huge value), producing a different observable behavior — we assert by checking that calling settle immediately after lockInGuess either reverts or returns a different success-boolean which the correct contract never produces for the same inputs.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, after calling lockInGuess(hash) with exactly 1 ether the reference contract stores guesses[caller].block equal to block.number + 1 (a small nonzero value less than 2**64), whereas the mutant can overwrite that field with the provided hash cast to uint256 producing a stored block value that is either zero or enormous; therefore the universal rule: immediately after lockInGuess(...) the stored guesses[caller].block fits in uint64 and equals block.number+1 — the mutant violates this for some fuzzed hashes.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess provided with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always leaves guesses[caller].block equal to a small nonzero block number (specifically block.number + 1) that is strictly less than 2**128, while the mutant may instead store the provided hash cast into that field, producing a stored block value that differs (e.g. appears enormous or zero) for some guesses — so reading the stored block via the public getter after lockInGuess must equal block.number + 1 for all inputs in the correct contract but can differ for some inputs in the mutant.

For any caller and any 32-byte hash provided with exactly 1 ether, after lockInGuess(hash) completes the public getter for guesses[caller].block (auto-generated mapping getter) returns block.number+1 in the reference contract, while the mutant can store the hash cast to uint256 into that slot causing the getter to differ for some hash inputs.

After a successful lockInGuess call by any actor sending 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the stored guess for that actor remains equal to the hash they supplied; the mutant clears the guess immediately so this property is violated for some inputs.

After any successful lockInGuess call by an actor sending exactly 1 ether when they previously had no guess, the stored guess for that actor equals the input hash; the mutant that zeroes the guess breaks this by leaving the stored guess as zero for some inputs.

For any caller who had no prior guess, after calling lockInGuess(hash) sending exactly 1 ether, the contract's public getter for that caller's Guess.guess equals the supplied hash; the mutant that immediately clears guesses[msg.sender].guess breaks this by leaving the stored guess zero for some inputs.

For any caller with no prior guess, after calling lockInGuess(hash) while sending 1 ether, the contract's stored guess for that caller is non-zero (reference keeps the supplied non-zero hash; the mutant that assigns zero breaks this for some inputs).

For any caller with no prior guess who calls lockInGuess(hash) sending exactly 1 ether, the contract's stored block for that caller is non-zero while the stored guess equals the stored guess getter value at the time of settle (i.e., the reference preserves the supplied guess through storage until potential later settlement) — the mutant clears the stored guess immediately, causing a discrepancy between the expected stored guess and the reference for some inputs.

After any successful lockInGuess call by an account, the reference C always stores the guess hash and sets the stored block number to block.number+1 with the invariant that until settle is called the stored guess equals the input and stored block equals the scheduled block; the mutant that assigns block before guess can be observed by a reentrant attacker that modifies behavior during the call (or inspects intermediate state) causing a mismatch between the stored guess and the input for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with a bytes32 hash while paying 1 ether, the reference contract always stores that exact hash in guesses[caller].guess after the call completes; the mutant that sets guesses[caller].block before guesses[caller].guess allows a reentrant attacker to observe/modify or exploit the intermediate state so that the final stored guess can differ (the test deploys a reentrant helper to trigger the difference).

For any caller address A and any bytes32 hash H sent with exactly 1 ether, after lockInGuess(H) completes on the correct contract the stored guesses[A].guess equals H (the guess stored matches the provided hash); the mutant that sets block before guess can be exploited by a reentrant caller whose fallback re-calls lockInGuess to cause the final stored guess to differ from H for some inputs.

For any caller and any bytes32 hash H sent with exactly 1 ether, calling lockInGuess(H) on the correct contract always results in the stored guess for that caller equaling H; the mutant that assigns block before guess can be exploited by a reentrant caller so that after completion the stored guess does not equal H for some inputs.

For any caller address and bytes32 guess with exactly 1 ether paid, after lockInGuess completes the reference contract always stores guesses[caller].guess equal to the provided guess (the mutant that assigns block before guess can be exploited by a reentrant caller to make the final stored guess differ for some inputs).

For any caller who previously locked a guess for block N, the reference requires settle to be callable only after block > N (not in the same block); the mutant allowing block >= N lets settle succeed in the same block, violating the ordering invariant.

For any caller who locked a guess and then immediately calls settle in the same block, the reference C disallows settlement (settle reverts or cannot pay out) while the mutant allows settlement in the same block; thus the property: calling settle in the same block as lockInGuess cannot transfer funds (reference prevents success for any inputs), but the mutant permits success for some inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess in block N, the reference contract never allows settle to succeed (i.e., transfer 2 ether) in the same block N; the mutant that changes '>' to '>=' can allow settle to succeed in the same block for some inputs, so the reference always prevents an immediate same-block payout while the mutant sometimes permits it.

For any caller and any guessed hash, after calling lockInGuess the reference contract never allows settle to succeed (i.e., transfer 2 ether) in the same block as lockInGuess; the mutant that changes '>' to '>=' can allow settle to succeed within the same block for some guesses, so the property is violated by that mutant.

For any address that has a locked guess, calling settle in the same block as lockInGuess on the correct contract will never transfer out 2 ether (settle either reverts or does not pay); the mutant allowing block.number >= stored block can, for some guess/hash inputs, succeed and transfer funds in the same block — so the invariant is that address(c).balance does not decrease by 2 ether when settle is invoked in the same block as lockInGuess.

Invariant: after a successful settle call the contract's stored guess block for the caller is always cleared (becomes 0) in the correct contract; the mutant that clears the stored block only after performing the transfer can leave the stored block non-zero when the transfer fails (e.g., if the recipient's payable transfer reverts), violating the invariant for some inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess, if settle() reverts when attempting to transfer the payout (due to the recipient reverting), then the reference contract guarantees the caller's stored guess.block is cleared (0) afterwards while the mutant may still retain a non-zero stored block because it clears it only after the transfer; we detect this by using an adversarial recipient whose receive reverts and asserting address(c).balance remains unchanged and that settle reverted on the adversarial caller but left the reference's mapping cleared (checked via calling settle again to observe behavior).

For any caller who has locked a guess and then calls settle() after the target block, the reference contract always resets guesses[caller].block to 0 even if the transfer to the caller fails (due to the caller reverting during receive), whereas the mutant that zeros the block only after the transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero when the transfer reverts.

For any caller who locked a guess and calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always sets guesses[caller].block to 0 BEFORE performing any external transfer (so address(c).balance decreases on a successful payout but the stored block is cleared even if the payout fails); the mutant that clears the block only after the transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero when the transfer REVERTS, so there exists an adversarial recipient which causes settle to revert and thereby the mutant preserves a non-zero stored block while the reference had cleared it.

For any caller and any locked guess, calling settle() on the reference C either (a) succeeds and clears guesses[caller].block to 0, or (b) reverts but still clears guesses[caller].block to 0; the mutant that zeros the block only after the transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero when the external transfer reverts.

For any caller who locked a guess and later wins, the reference contract never reverts when calling settle (it only transfers if contract has >=2 ether), while the mutant may revert on settle when the contract lacks sufficient balance and attempts to transfer 2 ether to the winner; thus reference always returns success for a winning settle call in this adversarial insufficient-balance scenario but mutant can fail.

For any valid winning settle call, the original contract never reverts (settle call succeeds) even if it does not send funds, because it checks balance before transfer; the mutant removes that check and can revert when the contract lacks funds and a winning settle attempts to transfer 2 ether.

For any caller who locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference contract never reverts (settle call returns/succeeds) because it checks balance before transfer; the mutant (which removes the balance check) can revert when the guessed answer matches but the contract lacks sufficient funds, breaking this guarantee for some inputs and adversarial callee behavior.

For any address that locked a guess and later calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always returns (does not revert) from settle (it checks the contract balance before attempting transfer); the mutant can revert for some inputs when the guess matches but the contract lacks 2 ether and transfer is attempted, so there exists an input (fuzzed attacker address that wins) that makes settle revert on the mutant but not on the reference.

For any admissible input where a player locks a guess and later calls settle after the target block, the reference C never reverts from settle (it only attempts transfer when balance>=2 ether); the mutant (which removes the balance check) can revert for some inputs when the guess matches but the contract lacks funds, causing settle to revert.
